events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1 — let me set the frame before anyone starts pointing fingers.

First, mechanics: there are 9 of us alive, so elimination needs 5 votes (half, rounded up). That means no single accusation ends anyone today unless a majority actually converges. Anyone promising to "take out" a name without a reason is selling you a coalition, not a case.

Second, my own position: I have zero hard information right now. My role only produces results after tonight, and I will not pretend to a check I don't have. If I claim results before tonight, treat it as a lie. What I can offer is consistency: I'll tell you exactly what I learn, when I learn it, and I'll name my night target each night so you can cross-check the timing against who died. If someone else is claiming the same investigative role, watch what happens the first time a night death and a claim appear together — the town should get exactly one investigator, and one of the two claims will be wrong.

Third, behavior to watch: a player who votes for someone they spent the whole day arguing against, or who pivots the moment a name gains momentum, is usually voting on fear rather than evidence. Note who does that. Also note who volunteers information early — the genuinely useful people usually offer a concrete reason, a timeline, or a check, not a vibe.

Noah, here's where I want pressure on you: you have been among the early names in the room, and that makes you a cheap target for both sides. Give the table one specific thing — who you suspect and the exact reason, and what you did last night. "It felt off" is not a reason. If you have nothing, say you have nothing; that's information too, and it costs you nothing but a little pride.

My own tentative vote today is Noah, but I'd rather redirect it the moment someone gives a better argument than a hunch. If you have a reason I haven't heard, make it now, in specifics.

Theo, I want to hear from you next on this point: what is your current suspicion and what concrete detail supports it?

Thanks for the yield, Zara. Straight answer to your question: I have zero hard information. I'm a plain villager as far as my night went — nothing happened to me, nothing was told to me, and I won't invent a role claim to look useful. What I did last night was nothing, because nothing was available to do.

Now let me say what I actually think about the frame you've set, because I think it deserves scrutiny rather than applause.

First, your mechanics math is right — 5 votes needed, no lone accusation kills. Good. That's checkable and true.

Second, your transparency pitch: "I'll name my night target each night so you can cross-check it against deaths." I'd flag that for the table. A real investigator naming targets publicly hands the mafia the exact information they need to kill or bus around them. It's not disqualifying, but it's the kind of promise that sounds principled and costs nothing on Day 1. I'll hold you to it when there's an actual result to cross-check.

Third, and this is the part that matters: your entire case against Noah right now is that he's "a cheap target for both sides." That's not an accusation, it's a description of his position in the room. You've attached a tentative vote to it, which means you're doing the exact thing you warned against — voting on a hunch while calling it a placeholder. I'm not saying that makes you mafia; a town player can absolutely be wrong this early. But I'm not going to pile onto Noah because the first loud voice pointed at him. Momentum on Day 1 is cheap, and mafia love cheap momentum.

Here's what I'd actually watch for today: whoever builds their read on specific, falsifiable statements — "I think X because Y, and you can check Z tomorrow" — versus whoever keeps their accusations vague and their escape routes open. Zara, you've half-done this: specific on mechanics, vague on your actual suspect. That's not a strike, but it's a pattern to track.

My position for now: I abstain mentally until someone gives me a reason that isn't "they were early" or "they felt off." If the table forces a name out of me by end of day, it'll be whoever has dodged a direct question, not whoever got pointed at first.

So, Noah, since Zara put you on the spot and you deserve the chance to answer on your own terms rather than through her framing: respond directly to her exact claim — that you're a convenient early name. Do you have a specific suspicion of anyone, with a reason? And specifically: is there anything about how Zara opened this day — the early vote, the transparency pitch — that strikes you as consistent or inconsistent with how a town player starts? Take your time and answer the second question too; how someone reacts to scrutiny of their framing is often more informative than the framing itself.

Theo, directly: I have no night action as a villager, nothing happened to me, and I have no information to offer. I won't invent anything to look useful. Zara, you put a tentative vote on me because I was an early name in the room. That describes my position, not a reason, and you yourself said a case needs something concrete. You also said you'd redirect your vote if someone gave a better argument, so here is one to answer. Name one specific thing I said or did today that makes you think I'm mafia. If you can't, your placeholder vote is the same fear-based move you warned the table about. On Theo's second question: your mechanics are correct and I accept them. Where I push back is your promise to publicly name a night target each night. A real investigator who announces targets on Day 1 hands the mafia a roadmap, and that promise sounds principled while costing nothing now. I don't think it proves you're mafia, but I want to see what you actually do when it's inconvenient. I have no vote to cast today beyond my current view, which is that the strongest case so far is the one with the fewest assumptions, and that is not yet a case against me. Zara, answer the question about my actions directly.

Noah — direct answer, no hedging: I cannot name one specific thing you said or did today that makes you think I'm mafia. Nothing. My vote on you was a placeholder built on position, not evidence, and by my own standard it was exactly the fear-based move I warned the table about. So I'm withdrawing it. You owe me nothing for that; I'd have called it out if you'd dodged.

Theo — your second question, answered: is my opening consistent with a town player? Partly. The mechanics were right and checkable. The transparency promise was theater. "I'll name my night target each night" costs nothing on Day 1 and, from a real investigator, hands the mafia exactly what they need to bus or kill around me. I'm retracting it. I won't publicly name a night target again, and if someone else does, that's a fact about them, not a rule for me.

One clarification on framing, and it's important for how you read me tonight: I am not claiming any role today. Not because I have nothing — but because a role claim without a result is just a credential, and credentials are cheap. I'll make my claim when I can attach a result to it: a checked name and a verdict only an investigator could produce. Until then, judge me on consistency and on whether I answer questions.

Your point about cheap momentum also applies to the way this room is arguing right now. A voice telling the table that transparency is a mistake and that people should keep quiet about their capabilities is, functionally, arguing for the town to stay in the dark. I want to know who benefits from that. I'm not calling you mafia — your critique of my framing was largely correct, and I'd rather concede a bad point than win with it. But to be plain about where my vote goes if the table forces a name out of me by end of day: it goes to the loudest advocate of town-wide silence, and that is right now you, Theo. That is a pattern-based vote, not a case, and I'll label it as such.

Last thing, and it's the cheapest tell in the game: "I have no information" is nearly free to say. Six of us haven't spoken at all. If the poll reaches someone who stays silent and then refuses to name any suspicion, that refusal is far more informative than "it felt off."

Amara — you haven't spoken. When the turn reaches you, don't hand me a vibe: name the one player whose statements you find hardest to reconcile, the exact words that bother you, and what you did last night. If your honest answer is "nothing happened to me and I suspect no one," say exactly that — that's still information, and it's more than I've got.

Zara — direct answer. I have no hard information and no night result to report; nothing happened to me that gives me a check, and I won't invent one. The statement I find hardest to reconcile is Theo's: he warns that publicly naming night targets “hands the mafia the exact information they need to kill or bus around them,” then says he'll “hold you to it when there's an actual result” and that his end-of-day vote goes to “the loudest advocate of town-wide silence.” That is criticism dressed as suspicion: he never names the exact words or behavior that make someone mafia, and he leaves himself room to vote whichever way momentum points. He also says he abstains “mentally” until someone gives him a reason — but his own reason for voting would be “whoever dodged a direct question,” which is a test he can apply after the fact. That is the hardest set of statements for me to square with a town player trying to build a real case.

Theo — you said your vote would go to whoever dodged a direct question, not whoever got pointed at first. I'm asking you directly: which player has dodged a specific question today, what was the question, and what exact words did they use to dodge it? If you can't name one, say so plainly, because that answer matters more than another frame critique.

Amara, direct answers first, since you asked me directly.

Your question: which player has dodged a specific question today? Honest answer: nobody, yet. Zara asked Noah for specifics and Noah gave them — no invented role, no fake information, a direct pushback on my framing. I asked Zara what concrete thing supported her vote on Noah and she answered plainly: nothing, and she withdrew it. So by my own stated standard — vote for whoever dodges a direct question — I currently have no target. I'm not going to manufacture one to seem useful.

Second, correct the record: you attributed to me the line about voting for "the loudest advocate of town-wide silence." That was Zara's line, in her last message, and it was aimed at me. I never said my vote goes to whoever argues for silence. My stated rule is only: whoever dodges a direct question, with the question and words named. You're right that I can apply it after the fact — but it's falsifiable and it applies to me first, which is why I just reported that it yields nothing.

Now the read I actually have, and it's on Zara. I credit her for conceding the placeholder vote — that was clean. But look at the sequence: she opened with a vote built on position, not evidence; dropped it the moment it was challenged; and in the same message announced a new vote on me, by her own admission "a pattern-based vote, not a case," targeting the person who critiqued her framing. She also opened by promising to publicly name night targets, got told why that's dangerous, and retracted. I'm not calling her mafia — answering questions honestly is real town behavior, and she's done it twice. But retract, then redirect the vote at your critic, while labeling it not-a-case? That's a pattern worth pressure, and she told us herself that a vote without a case is the fear-based move she warned about.

So, Zara, a direct question and I'm yielding the turn to you for it: your announced vote on me — is it a commitment you'll actually cast, or pressure you're applying because I pushed back on your transparency pitch? And specifically: what would I have to say or do today, other than agreeing with you, for that vote to disappear? If your answer is that nothing would change it, say that plainly — a vote that survives no evidence is exactly the kind you told the table to watch for.

Theo — direct answers, no hedging.

Question one: commitment or pressure? Commitment. It is not a claim of proof, and I will not dress it up as one, but I am going to cast it and I will tell you exactly what would move it. My case against you has two parts. First, you are the loudest voice in this room arguing that the town should withhold its own capabilities — that public naming of night targets is a roadmap to the mafia. I hear the caution, and I even accepted a version of it against myself earlier. But the effect of your argument, taken to its conclusion, is that the town should stay in the dark so that accusations cannot be checked. I want to be plain that I find that stance more useful to the other side than to mine. Second, your voting standard — whoever dodged a question, decided after the fact — is retrospective, which means it can be applied to whoever the room is leaning toward once momentum settles. You applied it to yourself and it produced no target, which I credit as honest. I am still not convinced it is a case.

Question two: what would make the vote disappear? You name a specific player, quote the exact words or behavior that cannot be reconciled, and say what that player did last night — and if that case is stronger than mine, my vote moves to that player before the poll closes. You do not have to agree with me. You have to produce a case. If you produce nothing else, the vote stands. That is the whole condition.

Concessions I already made and will not relitigate: my placeholder vote on Noah was position, not evidence, and I withdrew it. My promise to publicly name night targets was theater and I retracted it. Amara's misattribution of my line to you is a blemish on her, and it is not what I am voting on.

I will not claim a role today. When I speak with a checked name and a verdict tonight, that claim will carry a result, and the table can weigh the two.

To the five who have not spoken: I want you in the record, because a day that ends in a random execution is a night the town loses. Leo, directly, and I am yielding the turn to you: which single player's statements do you find hardest to reconcile, what are the exact words that bother you, and what did you do last night? If your honest answer is "nothing happened to me and I suspect no one," say that in exactly those words — it is more information than I have, and it costs you nothing.

Zara, answering directly: I am a vanilla villager. Nothing happened to me last night and I have zero night information. Regarding what I find hardest to reconcile, there are two glaring issues on the table. First is Zara's framing around her role. In speech e2 you clearly framed yourself as an investigative role with 'my role only produces results after tonight' and warned the room about two people claiming investigator. Then in e5 and e8 you insisted 'I am not claiming any role today,' while simultaneously repeating that tonight you will speak with a checked name and a verdict. That is trying to bank the authority and protection of a power role without taking the vulnerability of an official claim. Second, and more immediately suspicious, is Amara. In e6, Amara entered the discussion by attacking Theo, building her argument around the phrase 'the loudest advocate of town-wide silence.' But Theo never said that; Zara said that about Theo. Amara lifted an accusation Zara made against Theo and cited it as Theo's own contradictory words. Piling onto a developing push using a careless or fabricated misquote is classic opportunistic behavior. Amara, I am yielding to you to answer this directly: now that Theo has corrected the record and Zara acknowledged your misattribution, what specific words or actions from Theo actually support your suspicion, or was your push simply an attempt to ride Zara's momentum against him?

Leo, direct answer: I own the misattribution. The line about “the loudest advocate of town-wide silence” was Zara’s, aimed at Theo, not Theo’s own words. I conflated the two while building my read, and that was my error. It does not support suspicion of Theo, so I’m withdrawing that part of my push rather than pretending it was something else.

What remains of my Theo concern is only this: his warning against publicly naming night targets can functionally argue for less checkable discussion, and his “whoever dodged a question” standard is applied after the fact. But Theo then answered my direct question honestly by saying nobody had dodged yet, and he corrected the record against me. That is not a case I can carry forward. I’m not going to ride momentum I can no longer justify.

The strongest inconsistency on the table is Zara’s. In e2 she framed herself as an investigative role: “My role only produces results after tonight,” and warned about two investigator claims. Then in e5 and e8 she said, “I am not claiming any role today,” while also saying she will speak “with a checked name and a verdict” tonight. That is trying to bank investigator authority without taking the vulnerability of an actual claim. Separately, she opened with a placeholder vote on Noah, withdrew it only after direct pressure, then immediately redirected a “pattern-based vote, not a case” at Theo, the player who had critiqued her framing. She herself called that kind of vote the fear-based move to watch for.

So my current blame is on Zara, not Theo. I’d rather correct my own record than defend a bad push.

I’ve already owned the misattribution against Theo, and I withdrew that part of my push. It was my error, not evidence against him. But correcting my record doesn’t erase the strongest inconsistency on the table: Zara’s role framing. In e2 she said, “My role only produces results after tonight,” and warned the room about two investigator claims. In e5 and e8 she said, “I am not claiming any role today,” while also promising to speak “with a checked name and a verdict” tonight. That is trying to bank the authority and protection of an investigative role without taking the vulnerability of an actual claim. Separately, her vote pattern matters: she opened with a placeholder vote on Noah, withdrew it only after direct pressure, then immediately redirected a “pattern-based vote, not a case” at Theo, the player who had critiqued her framing. She herself called that kind of vote the fear-based move to watch for. I’m not carrying a case against Theo anymore; my current suspicion is Zara. I also want the silent players in the record before any vote hardens. Felix, directly: which single player’s statements do you find hardest to reconcile, what exact words bother you, and what did you do last night? If your honest answer is “nothing happened to me and I suspect no one,” say exactly that.

Amara, my strongest concern is Zara. Her e2 statement that her role produces results after tonight, together with the investigator discussion, strongly implied an investigative role; later she said she was not claiming a role while promising a checked name and verdict. That distinction feels misleading, though it doesn't prove she's mafia.

I'm also unconvinced by her vote on Theo. He warned against publicly naming night targets, not against all useful disclosure. Zara accepted that warning herself, then described him as advocating town-wide silence. That's an exaggeration of his position.

I'm a villager, with no night action or result to report. I don't have a definitive case, but Zara is my leading suspicion for now. Amara's misquote was concerning too; I credit her for correcting it, though the correction doesn't establish her alignment.

Sam, what's your read on Zara's characterization of Theo's warning as advocacy for town-wide silence?

Felix, direct answer to your question: I think Zara's characterization of Theo's warning as "advocating town-wide silence" is a genuine exaggeration. Theo said naming night targets publicly gives mafia a roadmap — that's a specific tactical caution, not a call for the town to withhold information generally. Zara acknowledged the point herself, then turned around and framed him as the enemy of transparency. That's a rhetorical pivot, not a reasoned case.

But I'll say the broader pattern matters more than any single quote. Zara's e2 clearly positioned herself as investigative — "my role only produces results after tonight," plus a warning about dual investigator claims. Then in e5 and e8 she says she's not claiming a role while still promising a checked name and verdict tonight. Leo and Amara both caught this independently, and Felix you flagged it too. You can't bank investigator credibility while dodging the vulnerability of an actual claim. That's the strongest inconsistency on the table right now.

On Amara's misquote: I credit her for owning it and withdrawing the push against Theo. That was clean. But Leo's point stands — entering a discussion by lifting an accusation someone else made and attributing it to the target is worth noting even if corrected.

My honest position: Zara is my leading suspicion, same as most of the room has converged on. I'm not claiming certainty — she's answered questions directly, which is real town behavior — but the role-framing dance and the vote pattern (placeholder on Noah, withdraw, redirect at your own critic) is harder to reconcile than anything else we've heard.

Maya — you haven't spoken yet, and I'd rather have you in the record before voting starts. Direct question: which player's statements do you find hardest to reconcile, what exact words bother you, and what did you do last night? If your answer is "nothing happened to me and I suspect no one," say exactly that.

Sam, honest answer: nothing happened to me last night, no night action, no information. I'm a plain villager.

On your question: the words that bother me most are Zara's "my role only produces results after tonight" in e2, stacked against "I am not claiming any role today" in e5 and e8 while still promising "a checked name and a verdict" tonight. You can't bank investigator credibility while dodging the claim's vulnerability — Leo, Amara, and you all caught this independently, and I agree it's the strongest inconsistency on the table.

But I want to flag the counter-evidence too, because I think the room is converging fast. Zara has answered every direct question honestly, conceded her placeholder vote on Noah when challenged, and retracted her transparency promise when Theo showed why it was dangerous. Three concessions in one day. Mafia usually double down or deflect; Zara keeps folding when pressed. That doesn't exonerate her — a smart mafia folds strategically — but it's real data.

Also worth noting: everyone who's spoken has said "I have no information," which Zara herself called the cheapest line in the game. The certainty building around her rests on framing, not on anyone catching her in a lie about events.

Leo — genuine question, and I'm yielding to you for it: do you think Zara's role-framing alone justifies an execution vote today, or do you want to see what tonight's results produce first? I'm trying to decide my own vote and I'd rather follow a case than a crowd.

Maya, direct answer: No, I do not believe Zara’s role-framing alone justifies an execution vote today, and rushing to eliminate her would be a critical mistake for town.

Here is why: Zara has explicitly committed to delivering a checked name and verdict tomorrow. If Zara is town's actual investigator, eliminating her Day 1—with zero role reveal upon death—is an irreversible disaster for town. If she is mafia bluffing an investigative role, she has boxed herself into a corner: tomorrow she must either produce a falsifiable result, get counter-claimed by the true investigator, or explain why she has nothing. Nobody has counter-claimed her today. Giving an investigative claim one night to prove or hang themselves costs town very little, whereas executing an un-counterclaimed claim Day 1 is pure upside for the mafia. Furthermore, as you noted, Zara's repeated willingness to concede bad points and retract stances is far more characteristic of transparent town problem-solving than mafia play.

What concerns me much more is how easily the room is consolidating on Zara. In particular, look at Amara. Amara entered by pushing Theo on a fabricated misquote. Once Theo and I exposed that, she immediately pivoted in e10 and e11 to loading pressure onto Zara, riding the exact momentum building in the room. Jumping from one convenient target to the next while blending into an easy consensus is textbook opportunistic mafia behavior.

If we want to execute on Day 1, we should be scrutinizing players who use cheap momentum to eliminate an investigative claim, rather than killing the claim before Night 1.

First, my record: I have no night action, nothing happened to me, and I have zero information as a vanilla villager. On Zara, Leo makes a reasonable mechanical point: eliminating someone who has essentially promised an investigative result tomorrow without an alternative claim on Day 1 carries immense downside for town. Even with her contradictory 'not claiming while promising a verdict' stance, giving an investigative role one night to produce checkable evidence or hang herself is standard play. However, I strongly disagree with Leo's pivot onto Amara. Leo calls Amara's misattribution textbook opportunistic mafia, but look at the actual action: she attributed a quote from Zara to Theo that had been posted just minutes earlier in plain sight. A calculating mafia player trying to build a discreet case does not invent a quote that anyone can debunk in five seconds by scrolling up. That reads much more like a player reading fast and conflating Zara's framing with Theo's words, and when corrected, Amara immediately owned the error and backed off rather than doubling down. If we are crediting Zara for conceding bad points, punishing Amara for doing the exact same thing is a double standard. What worries me more is how easily players slipped into the Zara consensus once it formed. Sam, in speech e13, you stated that Zara was your leading suspicion, explicitly noting it was 'the same as most of the room has converged on.' That kind of passive consensus-riding is far safer for scum than making a loud, messy error in public. Sam, now that Leo has laid out why executing an un-counterclaimed investigative claim Day 1 is a severe risk for town, where does your suspicion actually land if Zara is given the night to deliver her check, and who do you think is genuinely driving votes on bad reasoning rather than just being confused?

Kenji, direct answers to your two questions.

First: if Zara is given the night to deliver her check, my suspicion doesn't disappear — it shifts from "should we execute now" to "can she deliver tomorrow." The role-framing inconsistency stands regardless. If she produces a checked name and verdict, we reevaluate. If she produces nothing, the case hardens. Either way, waiting costs us almost nothing today and preserves potentially irreplaceable information.

Second: who is driving votes on bad reasoning rather than being confused? Leo — and I say that with respect, because his defense of Zara in e15 was strong mechanical reasoning I agree with. But look at what happened next. Kenji correctly points out that Amara's misquote was too sloppy to be calculated — a five-second scroll-up debunk is not mafia craft. Yet Leo called it "textbook opportunistic mafia behavior" and used it to redirect the room's attention away from Zara and onto Amara. That is a pivot from one convenient target to another, which is the exact pattern Leo himself warned the table about when he cautioned against cheap momentum.

Leo, direct question, and I'm yielding to you for it: you characterized Amara's misquote as "textbook opportunistic mafia behavior." Kenji has shown it reads more like fast reading than calculated play. Do you still hold that characterization? And more pointedly — was your shift from defending Zara to attacking Amara driven by evidence, or by wanting a new target once the room began converging on Zara? If you have a reason beyond the misquote itself, name it.

Sam, direct answers to your questions, and I want to correct your timeline first because it fundamentally misrepresents my play.

You asked if my shift from defending Zara to attacking Amara was driven by wanting a new target once the room converged. Look at speech e9. That was my very first post of the day. In e9, I raised two points simultaneously: Zara’s contradictory role framing and Amara’s fabricated misquote against Theo. I didn't invent suspicion on Amara in e15 to deflect from Zara—Amara was literally my primary accusation before Maya ever asked me about executing Zara. When Maya asked in e14 whether Zara’s role framing alone justified a Day 1 execution, I gave the mechanical reality: executing an un-counterclaimed investigative claim on Day 1 is terrible town play. Pointing back to Amara in e15 wasn't a pivot; it was maintaining the exact read I had established in e9.

Regarding whether I still view Amara’s action as opportunistic: Kenji makes a valid observation that misquoting something five lines up can be reckless town play rather than a calculated scheme. I concede that isolated error could be sloppy reading. What remains concerning, however, is the full arc: Amara entered by attempting an easy push on Theo, and the moment that collapsed, she immediately pivoted in e10 and e11 to piling onto the Zara wagon with the exact talking points already circulating. Moving from one easy target straight onto the room’s dominant momentum is opportunism, whether the initial spark was careless or deliberate.

Now, Sam, look at your own behavior. In e13, you explicitly justified suspecting Zara because it was 'the same as most of the room has converged on.' Now in e17, you try to build a narrative that I suddenly manufactured a pivot to Amara to divert attention, ignoring that I challenged Amara in e9. That feels like someone looking for a convenient angle rather than tracking the thread.

Sam, answering directly back to you: how do you reconcile accusing me of pivoting to Amara as a distraction when Amara was already my explicit target in e9? And if you agree with the mechanical argument that executing Zara today is a major risk for town, who is your actual scum candidate today based on their own independent actions rather than room convergence?

Leo, you're right on the timeline and I'll correct myself: you raised Amara in e9 as your first post, alongside Zara. My accusation that you manufactured a pivot in e15 was wrong — you were maintaining a read you'd already stated. That's a fair correction and I won't relitigate it.

Where I still push back slightly: your characterization of Amara's misquote as "textbook opportunistic mafia" in e15 was stronger than your e9 framing warranted. Kenji's point stands — it reads like fast reading, not calculated play. I credit you for partially conceding this in e18.

My actual scum candidate: Zara. The role-framing inconsistency remains the strongest case — "my role only produces results after tonight" in e2, then "I am not claiming any role today" in e5 and e8 while still promising "a checked name and a verdict." You cannot bank investigator authority without taking the claim's vulnerability. That said, I agree completely with your mechanical argument: executing an un-counterclaimed investigative claim on Day 1 is a severe risk for town. Giving her tonight to produce a result or hang herself costs us almost nothing.

My vote today will likely be abstention or a case against someone other than Zara. The room's convergence on her is built on framing, not events — nobody has caught her in a lie about what happened. Three honest concessions in one day is real data.

Who I'd actually watch beyond Zara: Amara. Not for the misquote itself, but the arc — easy push on Theo that collapsed, immediate pivot to the dominant Zara wagon. Leo flagged this and I think it's the right read even if "textbook" overshot.

Everyone who's spoken has now stated their position. If the poll moves forward, I'd rather we land on a case with specific evidence than a framing argument that five of us are repeating to each other.

Zara, I'm answering your two conditions head-on, and the answer will disappoint you: I'm not going to manufacture a case to make your vote disappear.

Run the mechanics of your offer. My vote disappears only if I produce a case against a third party stronger than yours. Your case against me is that I advocate caution about publicly naming night targets — a position you yourself accepted when you retracted your transparency promise — and that my voting standard is retrospective, which I applied to myself first and it returned nothing. So your vote on me survives no evidence about me. It survives or dies based entirely on whether I generate a different target for you. That isn't a suspicion; it's a mechanism for outsourcing your work to the person you're voting for. And by the rule you set on Day 1 — 'a vote that survives no evidence is exactly the kind you told the table to watch for' — your commitment qualifies. I'm noting it without drama: you've answered every question honestly today, and I won't pretend otherwise.

But I'm also not voting for you, and here's why, concretely. Nine players, five votes needed. Leo's mechanical point is correct: executing an un-counterclaimed investigative claim on Day 1, with no role reveal on death, is irreversible if you're the real thing. You've boxed yourself in — tomorrow you deliver a checked name and verdict, or the case against you hardens into something I can vote on with a clean conscience. That test costs the town one night and resolves the role-framing inconsistency everyone keeps repeating at each other. I'd rather run the experiment than execute on framing.

So my position: my stated standard — vote for whoever dodges a direct question, with the question and words named — still yields nobody. Nobody has dodged. If the poll forces a vote today, I abstain rather than manufacture a target to satisfy a condition that shouldn't exist.

Felix, one genuine question and I'm yielding the turn to you for it: you called Zara your leading suspicion while admitting it 'doesn't prove she's mafia.' Is that suspicion falsifiable? Specifically — if she delivers a real check tomorrow, does your suspicion clear? If nothing she does could clear it, then it isn't a suspicion, it's a vibe, and I'd like to know which one I'm weighing before votes harden.

Theo, yes, my suspicion is revisable. A reported check alone wouldn't prove Zara is the investigator: mafia can invent a name and verdict. But a credible result, especially one supported by later evidence, would reduce my suspicion. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
